title: Runway moves into your editing timeline
description: New plugins bring AI generation to Premiere Pro and After Effects. What changes for editors—and what still uses credits.
takeaway: Runway announced Adobe plugins on September 8. The download is free; generation uses your Runway plan and credits.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: The render is ready. Now comes the less glamorous job: getting it into your edit, naming the revision and checking that it matches the sequence. That handoff is the reason to look at Runway's Adobe plugins. Here is what the announcement actually changes, what still costs credits and what to check before using it on a deadline.

sections.heading: What was announced
sections.content: Runway's September 8 changelog introduces panels for Adobe Premiere Pro and After Effects on macOS and Windows. The company says editors can generate images and video, restyle existing footage and place results in their sequence or composition. The release is listed for paid plans.

sections.heading: What editors can do
sections.content: The plugin page describes generation, video editing, upscaling and access to existing library assets. Installation covers both Adobe applications. Runway directs users to open the panel through Window → Extensions → Runway and sign in. Duration and resolution depend on the selected model.

sections.heading: Our take: test the handoff first
sections.content: The useful question is whether the panel reduces the work between a generation and an approved shot. Before using it on a deadline, duplicate a short project and try one complete round trip. This is an editorial evaluation plan, not a claim that we have tested the release.
subpoints: Check the returned clip's frame rate, dimensions and color handling against your sequence.
Record credits charged for the model and settings you actually use.
Check how revisions are named and stored before handing the project to another editor.
Keep the original media so a restyle can be reversed.

sections.heading: Free download does not mean free rendering
sections.content: Runway says the installer is free and generations use account credits. An in-editor interface changes the workflow, not the need to budget for rejected takes. Use your own accepted-shot rate when estimating costs. We have not independently measured plugin speed or output quality.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Next, turn one missing shot in your edit into a clear prompt. Read [AI video prompts: six examples and a repeatable workflow](/create/ai-video-prompt-guide-examples).

title: ComfyUI brings 3D generation into the graph
description: Native Trellis.2 and Pixal3D support adds a new path from an image to a mesh. Production readiness still needs checking.
takeaway: Comfy Org announced native Trellis.2 and Pixal3D support on August 31, with updated 3D loading, preview and export tools.

sources.title: Trellis.2 and Pixal3D Are Now Native in ComfyUI

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: A generated mesh is only useful if it survives the next step in your project. Before treating native 3D generation as a shortcut, decide where the asset needs to go: a background render, an animation or an interactive scene. This announcement is worth understanding through that destination, not just through an impressive preview.

sections.heading: What changed
sections.content: Comfy Org says both models now run as core nodes, with rebuilt 3D tools and mesh post-processing. Its announcement describes an expanded material workflow. The integration reduces reliance on separate custom-node installations for this specific pipeline.

sections.heading: Start with a small asset
sections.content: The announcement points readers to ComfyUI 0.34.0, templates and model download instructions. Use the linked guide for the current requirements. We have not measured memory use or rendering time on a local GPU.

sections.heading: Our take: evaluate the exported mesh
sections.content: A good preview is the beginning of an asset check. Use a simple object with an obvious front and back, then bring the output into the application where you intend to use it. Define a usable result before changing settings.
subpoints: Inspect the silhouette from viewpoints absent from the source image.
Check thin parts, holes and hidden surfaces.
Inspect material maps under neutral lighting.
Record cleanup time as part of the cost of an accepted asset.

sections.heading: Where this fits
sections.content: Our starting point would be a prototype asset with a modest cleanup budget. A close-up hero prop has different acceptance criteria from a background object. Keep the source image, workflow and exported mesh together so you can repeat a promising run. This is workflow advice, not a measured ranking of 3D models.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: New to the graph? Build one working image workflow before adding another kind of output. Read [ComfyUI beginner guide: your first image and common fixes](/workflow/comfyui-beginner-first-workflow-guide).

title: Comfy MCP connects agents to local workflows
description: Comfy Org open-sourced its local MCP server. Agents can inspect an installation and help build workflows around available models and nodes.
takeaway: Comfy Org's August 18 announcement extends its MCP connection to local installations and links to the open-source server.

sources.title: Open Sourcing Comfy MCP on Local

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: You have a workflow idea, a folder full of models and no desire to explain your installation from scratch. Comfy MCP is interesting because it connects an agent to that local context. Read the announcement with one question in mind: which small, inspectable task would you trust the connection to help with?

sections.heading: What the local connection adds
sections.content: Comfy Org describes a connection that exposes local hardware, installed models and loaded nodes to an agent. The announcement says it supports building, editing and running workflows, alongside the existing cloud connection.

sections.heading: Why installation context matters
sections.content: Our reading: a workflow is useful only when its dependencies match the machine that runs it. Knowing which models and nodes are installed can make a proposed graph easier to inspect. This does not establish that a generated graph will produce an acceptable image or finish within a particular time.

sections.heading: A practical first task
sections.content: Start with a workflow that already produces a known result. Ask for one small change, inspect the graph and compare its output with the baseline. This gives you a clearer evaluation than asking an agent to assemble an unfamiliar production pipeline in one step.
subpoints: Save the original workflow and model filenames.
Choose one visible change, such as output dimensions or a prompt variation.
Review requested installs and downloads before applying them.
Record whether the change is repeatable using the saved graph.

sections.heading: Where to begin
sections.content: The release links to the official setup guide and public repository. Follow those current instructions for connection details. FyreLinkz has not independently benchmarked the server or verified every supported client.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Create a baseline workflow you understand before asking an agent to change it. Read [ComfyUI beginner guide: your first image and common fixes](/workflow/comfyui-beginner-first-workflow-guide).

title: MiniMax vs Seedance vs Higgsfield: choose for your next shot
description: Compare AI video tools by controls, delivery requirements, accepted takes and the real cost of finishing a shot.
takeaway: Direct Answer: Choose MiniMax/Hailuo when you need rich physical motion and fluid camera movement from text prompts; choose Seedance when keyframe continuity and storyboard constraints dictate the cut; choose Higgsfield for mobile-first camera templates. If your production requires multi-camera sync or NLE timeline integration, Runway Gen-3/4 remains the industry standard.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: Intended reader: Video editors, creative directors and solo creators deciding where to spend generation credits for a multi-shot project. Practical outcome: A 4-step evaluation sheet to test tools against your actual creative brief before committing to monthly tiers. Three attractive demo reels do not tell you which service will finish your project. Start with the shot you need: a product turn, a character action or a moving background. This guide provides a reproducible selection framework, not a synthetic league table.

sections.heading: Separate the platform from the model
sections.content: A creative platform can offer several models behind one interface. Runway's plugin documentation, for example, lists multiple video models in the same panel. Compare the selected model version, input mode and output settings; do not assume a result belongs to the platform's own model.

sections.heading: Build a shot brief before a shortlist
sections.content: Write down the result you need: subject, camera movement, duration, framing and details that must stay stable. A product turntable and a dialogue shot need different controls. Our suggested brief is small enough to use across services without changing the creative goal.
subpoints: Input: text only, starting frame, references or an existing clip.
Delivery: dimensions, duration, frame rate and audio.
Acceptance: identity, readable details, camera path and editability.
Constraints: turnaround time, available credits and project usage terms.
checklist: Lock delivery aspect ratio (16:9, 9:16, 1:1) and target duration before generating.
Separate subject description from background environment in the prompt text.
Specify exact camera vector (e.g., "dolly forward at steady pace", not "cool camera move").
Prepare an uncompressed 1080p starting frame for image-to-video runs.
Enforce a strict 3-take limit per prompt variant before revising the input image.

sections.heading: Keep a fair comparison log
sections.content: Use the same brief, save the actual input and record every attempt. Inspect the complete clip at delivery size. Log why each rejection failed instead of showing only the best take. A useful record contains model version, date, settings, credits charged and accepted seconds. Without that record, a precise quality ranking is not reproducible.

sections.heading: Calculate cost from accepted footage
sections.content: Divide generation spend by accepted seconds, then multiply by 60. For an illustrative example, spending $12 across a batch that yields 30 accepted seconds gives $24 per usable minute. This is arithmetic, not a quoted vendor price or measured rejection rate. Include upscaling, editing and audio costs separately. For practical prompt structures and camera directions to try in your next shot, see our companion [AI video prompting guide](/create/ai-video-prompt-guide-examples).

sections.heading: Know when to stop rerolling
sections.content: Decide the rejection budget before a test. If repeated outputs fail on the same critical detail, try a simpler shot, a different input method or a conventional editing step. A model that produces an impressive demo may still be a poor fit for one tightly constrained brief. Compare the cost of solving that brief, not the number of features on a landing page.

sections.heading: Correction to the earlier comparison
sections.content: This page previously presented sample clips and precise cost and quality claims without adequate provenance. Those benchmark claims have been withdrawn. This replacement is a decision framework informed by linked documentation. We have not established a universal winner among MiniMax, Seedance and Higgsfield.

sections.heading: Use a shortlist with explicit pass and fail rules
sections.content: Build a small comparison sheet before you pay for several services. Give each candidate the same job and record whether it satisfies the essential requirements. Our suggested columns are: supported input, control needed, delivery format, rights check, observed failure and usable output. Mark unknown information as unknown. A feature mentioned in a platform announcement does not establish that it is included in your selected plan or available through the interface you intend to use.
subpoints: For a product shot, prioritize stable shape and a usable opening and closing frame.
For a character scene, define which visible identity details must survive the motion.
For an atmospheric background, decide how much variation the edit can tolerate.

rows: Dynamic physical action & complex fluid scenes
Strict continuity between established storyboard frames
Occasional morphing on rapid camera rotations
Social-first character moves and rapid style testing
Fixed aspect ratios & limited custom NLE integration
Higher credit consumption per high-resolution render

sections.heading: Example: plan a short product sequence
sections.content: Suppose your edit needs an establishing shot, a close detail and a final hero view. Treat these as three jobs instead of one prompt asking for a complete commercial. Draft the camera position, subject action and desired cut for each shot. Then decide which shots actually need generation: a still with a simple editorial move may serve one of them. This example is a planning exercise, not a tested comparison. The point is to spend on the missing footage rather than paying to regenerate material your edit already has.

sections.heading: Track the cost of finishing, not only generating
sections.content: Alongside generation charges, record time spent selecting takes, repairing defects, upscaling, creating audio and assembling the edit. These costs depend on your workflow; a public credit table cannot settle them. Keep subscription overhead separate from the marginal cost of another attempt. If the deadline is fixed, a tool that produces acceptable material earlier may be a better choice even when its listed clip price is higher. Revisit the decision after a real project using saved results, not a promotional output selected by the vendor.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Put your shortlist to work: choose one of six original shot prompts and adapt it to your brief. Read [AI video prompts: six examples and a repeatable workflow](/create/ai-video-prompt-guide-examples).

title: FLUX in ComfyUI: a practical workflow and LoRA checklist
description: Choose a FLUX.1 starting point, understand the graph and introduce LoRAs after a reproducible baseline works.
takeaway: Direct Answer: To run FLUX.1 without CUDA out-of-memory errors on 12GB–16GB consumer GPUs, load FLUX.1 dev in FP8 (or GGUF Q4_K_M / Q8_0) using ComfyUI’s native UNETLoader and DualCLIPLoader, offload CLIP and T5 to CPU RAM, and clamp inference to 20–25 steps with Euler sampler. Only introduce LoRA nodes after validating this baseline.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: Intended reader: Creators running local RTX 3060/4070/4080 GPUs seeking photorealistic outputs from FLUX.1. Practical outcome: A crash-free node setup that loads weights efficiently and accepts LoRAs without breaking latent dimensions. Your base image looks promising, but the moment you add a LoRA, several other things change too. Was it the model, the prompt or the new component? Build a baseline you can return to, then make one deliberate change.

sections.heading: Choose the model deliberately
sections.content: Black Forest Labs identifies FLUX.1 dev as a 12-billion-parameter model. Its model card links a specific non-commercial model license and separately describes permitted output uses. FLUX.1 schnell lists Apache 2.0. Treat model licensing and output usage as separate checks; read the terms for the exact files you download.

sections.heading: Begin with the official inference example
sections.content: ComfyUI's FLUX.1 tutorial supplies a workflow and explains the model components. Follow its file placement instructions, load the graph and confirm that selected files match the example. An inference workflow generates an image from existing weights; it does not train a new LoRA.

sections.heading: Save a reproducible baseline
sections.content: Use one prompt and fixed settings until a complete image succeeds. Store the graph alongside a short environment note. This makes it easier to separate a missing file from a creative change or incompatible custom node.
subpoints: Record ComfyUI version and selected model filenames.
Save prompt, seed, dimensions and sampling settings.
Record peak memory and elapsed time on your own hardware.
Keep the first working output as a reference.
checklist: Download clip_l.safetensors and t5xxl_fp8_e4m3fn.safetensors into ComfyUI/models/clip/.
Download flux1-dev.safetensors into ComfyUI/models/unet/ or models/checkpoints/.
Download ae.safetensors into ComfyUI/models/vae/.
Connect DualCLIPLoader (clip_l + t5xxl) to CLIPTextEncode with clip_type set to "flux".
Set KSampler: steps=20, cfg=1.0, sampler_name=euler, scheduler=simple.
Run a single test generation at 1024x1024 to verify VRAM allocation before loading LoRA weights.

sections.heading: Add a LoRA as one controlled change
sections.content: Add one compatible LoRA, compare it with the baseline and record its strength. Check the author's base-model requirements. Avoid stacking unfamiliar adapters while debugging. For training, treat dataset preparation, trainer compatibility and evaluation images as a separate project. A working generation graph does not validate a training configuration.

sections.heading: Memory savings need a measured trade-off
sections.content: The FLUX.1 dev example demonstrates CPU offloading to reduce GPU memory use. That does not establish a universal minimum VRAM figure. Dimensions, extra nodes, precision and other resident workloads change what fits. Compare a small fixed job before and after a memory-saving change; preserve its output and timing.

rows: Commercial paid API · When local hardware is unavailable

sections.heading: A useful stopping point
sections.content: Your first milestone is a saved graph that another person can reopen with the same files and understand. Add a short note describing what each extra adapter contributes. Only then scale dimensions, batch size or training complexity. This guide is documentation-based; it does not claim a tested speedup on a particular GPU.

sections.heading: Keep an experiment card beside the workflow
sections.content: Our suggested experiment card has six fields: model files, workflow version, input or prompt, changed setting, expected effect and observed result. Fill it in before introducing a LoRA. This makes it harder to mistake a different prompt, seed or resolution for the effect of the LoRA itself. A fixed seed is helpful within a controlled setup, but does not guarantee identical outputs after hardware or software changes. Preserve the complete baseline rather than only a screenshot of the nodes.

sections.heading: Separate inference from a training decision
sections.content: Using an existing LoRA and training your own are different projects. Before training, define the visual behavior you cannot obtain from your current workflow and collect example material you have permission to use. Reserve some examples for evaluation rather than treating every pleasing result as proof of generalization. This is a planning recommendation; the exact data preparation and training settings belong to the selected training tool and model license. Do not start with a promised universal rank or step count.

sections.heading: Choose the next change by the problem you can see
sections.content: If the image is compositionally wrong, investigate the input and conditioning before optimizing memory. If the workflow fails to load, verify required files and component compatibility before rewriting the prompt. If the result changes after an update, compare the saved baseline on the new environment before adding more nodes. Solve one category of failure at a time. The useful milestone is not the longest graph: it is an output you can explain, reproduce closely enough for the project and hand off with clear notes.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: If the graph still feels unfamiliar, start with the first-image walkthrough. Read [ComfyUI beginner guide: your first image and common fixes](/workflow/comfyui-beginner-first-workflow-guide).

imageAlt: Conceptual diagram of FLUX.1 latent diffusion architecture with LoRA weight adapter nodes.

title: Building a local AI PC: check VRAM before buying a GPU
description: A workload-first guide to GPU memory, model offloading, multi-GPU assumptions and the costs beyond a graphics-card specification.
takeaway: Direct Answer: For local AI in 2026, VRAM capacity strictly determines what models you can run without system slowdowns. 16GB (RTX 4070 Ti Super) is the minimum baseline for quantized FLUX and 8B LLMs; 24GB (RTX 3090 / 4090) is the sweet spot for full-fidelity diffusion and 14B–32B models; running two GPUs splits workloads across processes but does NOT merge VRAM into a single memory pool for standard ComfyUI runs.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: Intended reader: Creators and developers building a dedicated local machine for generative image/video diffusion and local LLM inference. Practical outcome: A hardware dimensioning worksheet covering VRAM, PCIe lane bifurcation, power headroom, and system RAM ratios. A graphics card can look perfect on a specification sheet and still be wrong for the model you want to run. Before building a shopping cart, write down your actual workflow, output size and waiting-time limit.

sections.heading: Specify the workload first
sections.content: List the exact model, precision, context or image dimensions, and concurrency you expect. A workstation for one image at a time has a different budget from one serving several long conversations. Ask whether the software loads your intended configuration and whether its measured throughput meets the job.

sections.heading: Capacity and speed answer different questions
sections.content: NVIDIA lists the RTX 4090 with 24 GB of GDDR6X memory. Capacity is a useful constraint, not evidence that every 24 GB workflow performs equally well. Account for runtime memory beyond stored weights. Do not compare cards using a model-size number alone.

rows: Budget FLUX FP8 / SDXL / 8B LLMs with 8k context
Most cost-effective 24GB entry point for heavy ComfyUI graphs
Fastest consumer batch inference & local video diffusion
Local LLM tensor parallelism (vLLM / Ollama 70B Q4)

sections.heading: Offloading is a software strategy
sections.content: Hugging Face Accelerate documents distributing large-model weights across GPU, CPU and disk when needed. Placement lets a workload use several memory tiers; it is not the same as giving one GPU a larger allocation. The actual framework and model must support your plan.

sections.heading: Before buying a second GPU
sections.content: Treat a dual-card machine as an integration project. Start with the inference engine and end with the physical build. Do not buy an interconnect on the assumption that its presence makes every model use both cards.
subpoints: Confirm application support for the required multi-GPU mode.
Check motherboard slot spacing and electrical lane allocation.
Use the card maker's power, connector and clearance requirements.
Allow airflow around both cards and the rest of the system.
Find a repeatable result for the exact configuration, or test comparable rented hardware.

sections.heading: Budget for a month of real work
sections.content: Compare acquisition cost, electricity, storage and maintenance time with the cloud spend you expect to avoid. For a small irregular workload, ownership may save less than a headline hourly comparison suggests. For a repeatable daily workload, measure utilization and accepted output. This guide makes no benchmark or payback-period claim.

sections.heading: A purchase checklist you can actually use
sections.content: Bring a written workload to the purchase decision: required files, supported runtime, a known working command or graph, expected volume and an acceptable turnaround. Check current local prices and warranty terms. Keep enough budget for the supporting machine instead of spending everything on a card that the rest of the system cannot accommodate.
checklist: Verify System RAM is at least 2x your GPU VRAM (minimum 32GB–64GB DDR5 for model swapping).
Check PSU capacity has at least 150W headroom above total system peak load (850W for single 4090, 1200W+ for dual).
Ensure motherboard supports PCIe 4.0/5.0 x8/x8 bifurcation if planning dual-GPU expansion.
Choose NVMe storage with at least 2TB Gen4 capacity for fast checkpoint loading (3–5 GB/s reads).
Measure physical GPU clearance (length, slot thickness, and 12VHPWR bend radius) in the case.

sections.heading: Write three workloads before making a shopping list
sections.content: Use one everyday task, one demanding task and one task you might need later. Record the exact model or workflow, target output and whether simultaneous jobs are required. A machine chosen for occasional experimentation can have different priorities from one used for a daily production queue. Treat the future task as a separate budget decision rather than assuming it justifies every expensive component today. This worksheet is our planning method, not a measured hardware benchmark.

sections.heading: Ask for evidence you can compare
sections.content: When evaluating a benchmark, look for the complete configuration and workload. Model version, precision, context length or image dimensions, batch size and software settings can change the meaning of a speed number. A result without this context is a lead for further research, not a purchase guarantee. Prefer a test you can reproduce using the same job you need to run. Keep loading time and repeated-run time separate if both affect your working day.

sections.heading: Make the purchase reversible where possible
sections.content: Check the seller's return terms and the physical compatibility of the whole build before ordering. List case clearance, power connectors, cooling space and the expansion slots your actual configuration will use. Plan where models, project inputs and backups will live. After assembly, run the smallest known working workflow, then your everyday workload, before adding the demanding one. Record failures and actual operating costs during this trial so the next upgrade follows evidence rather than a specification headline.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Complete the workstation around the work you do every day: check monitor readability before chasing refresh-rate numbers. Read [A 4K monitor for coding: check text before refresh rate](/hardware/best-4k-144hz-monitors-for-programming).

title: Choosing an SDXL checkpoint: a fair comparison checklist
description: A repeatable evaluation sheet for portrait and product workflows: fixed prompts, compatible settings and recorded failure cases.
takeaway: Use the same brief and record every result. Community example images are inspiration, not a controlled comparison.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: One beautiful sample image can hide the exact problem your project keeps hitting. Instead of downloading every promising checkpoint, make a small test set that includes your difficult cases. This guide helps you compare repeatable results, record failures and choose a model for your own portrait or product workflow.

sections.heading: Start from the model family
sections.content: Stability AI's SDXL model card describes the base model and an optional refiner workflow. Use it to understand the starting architecture before comparing community checkpoints. A checkpoint author's recommended settings may differ; record those differences rather than silently giving one model an easier test.

sections.heading: Make a small evaluation sheet
sections.content: Choose a few tasks you actually need, such as a head-and-shoulders portrait, a full-body pose and an object on a plain background. Decide what counts as acceptable before generating. This is our proposed evaluation method, not an existing benchmark.
subpoints: Use consistent prompts and dimensions for the initial comparison.
Record the checkpoint version, seed, sampler and any adapters.
Keep failed images alongside successful ones.
Repeat a promising result across more than one seed.

sections.heading: Separate style from reliability
sections.content: A dramatic lighting style can make a result look polished while hiding details you need to inspect. Look at small objects, facial details, repeated patterns and areas that require later editing. Mark defects by task. A checkpoint that suits one portrait style is not automatically the best choice for a product catalog.

sections.heading: Keep usage terms with the files
sections.content: Check the terms on the exact checkpoint and any adapter before using them in a client workflow. Do not assume that all files sharing a base architecture have identical terms. This page replaces an unsupported ranking of RealVisXL, Juggernaut and CyberRealistic; no measured winner is claimed.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Use the same baseline-first approach when experimenting with FLUX and LoRAs. Read [FLUX in ComfyUI: a practical workflow and LoRA checklist](/create/comfyui-flux-lora-training-and-inference-guide).

title: Is a new AI model worth switching to? A practical checklist
description: Turn a model announcement into a useful decision: verify availability, controls, costs and whether it improves your actual workflow.
takeaway: A release announcement proves an announced capability. It does not prove an improvement on your own task.

sources.title: Open Sourcing Comfy MCP on Local

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: Another model announcement arrives before you have finished learning the last one. You do not need to rebuild your workflow every time. First identify the part of your current job that is slow, unreliable or missing a needed control. Then use the checklist below to decide whether the release deserves a small trial.

sections.heading: Verify the exact release
sections.content: Runway's changelog records model and product updates with dates and plan labels. Comfy Org separately documents local workflow integrations. Use original release notes to distinguish a new model from a new interface, provider integration or availability change.

sections.heading: Write the migration question
sections.content: Instead of asking whether a model is the best, write what your present workflow cannot do. Perhaps you need a particular reference input, a longer shot or less manual cleanup. A specific problem makes the comparison falsifiable: either the new workflow handles the brief within your budget or it does not.

sections.heading: Check four things before paying
sections.content: Build a short record from the vendor's current documentation. Keep the access date because interfaces, model aliases and plan limits can change.
subpoints: Availability: your region, account tier and intended API or app.
Controls: inputs, duration, aspect ratio, output format and editing options.
Cost: what consumes credits, what is billed on failure and which steps are extra.
Fit: your accepted-result criteria and downstream editing requirements.

sections.heading: Run a small switch test
sections.content: Save a baseline job and try the alternative with the same brief. Count the time to inspect, revise and export—not just generation time. Keep your existing workflow until the alternative produces a repeatable benefit. Earlier unsupported frontier-model rankings have been replaced by this evaluation guide.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: For a concrete example, apply the checklist to your next AI video shot. Read [MiniMax vs Seedance vs Higgsfield: choose for your next shot](/create/ai-video-generation-matrix-minimax-higgsfield-seedance).

imageAlt: Conceptual editorial illustration of multidimensional AI model benchmark radar chart and metrics.

title: Qdrant vs Weaviate vs Milvus vs Pinecone: what to compare
description: Choose a vector database with a workload sheet that covers retrieval quality, filters, memory, operating costs and recovery.
takeaway: There is no useful latency winner without a dataset, retrieval target, hardware configuration and query workload.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: Your search demo finds a useful paragraph. The harder questions arrive when you add real filters, more documents and a recovery requirement. Before selecting a vector database, write down those conditions. This guide helps you design a comparison around retrieval quality and operational work, without pretending one benchmark fits every application.

sections.heading: Begin with the retrieval problem
sections.content: The linked documentation describes the platforms and their indexing concepts. Before comparing implementation choices, define your records, vector dimensions, metadata filters and expected query mix. A demonstration with unfiltered vectors does not establish performance for filtered production traffic.

sections.heading: Make the measurements comparable
sections.content: Use the same dataset and relevance evaluation across candidates. Record configuration changes that trade retrieval quality for speed. Keep a reproducible query set so a faster run is not simply an easier one.
subpoints: Data volume, vector dimensions and metadata distribution.
Target retrieval quality and number of results returned.
Concurrent requests, update rate and filtering conditions.
Index build time, steady-state memory and recovery behavior.

sections.heading: Count operating costs beyond the index
sections.content: For self-hosting, include the infrastructure and the work of upgrades, backups and incident response. For a managed service, calculate the current billed units for your workload, including storage and reads or writes where applicable. Compare a month of expected usage; this page intentionally does not reuse unverified dollar or p99 latency figures.

sections.heading: A sensible shortlist process
sections.content: Start with the platform your team can operate competently, then test the requirement most likely to disqualify it. A useful proof of concept includes a restore or rebuild, not only a successful query. Keep the configuration and evaluation sheet with the decision so the choice can be revisited as volume changes.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Check the other half of retrieval quality: whether your extraction pipeline preserves the source material you need. Read [Firecrawl or Playwright for RAG? Choose the missing step](/stack/ai-web-scraping-pipelines-firecrawl-playwright-rag).

imageAlt: Conceptual illustration of high-dimensional vector embeddings, nearest-neighbor clusters, and graph indexing.

title: Firecrawl vs Playwright for RAG: which problem are you solving?
description: Separate page access, extraction and retrieval. Compare a managed extraction service with a browser workflow using a small evaluation set.
takeaway: Direct Answer: Use Playwright when your RAG pipeline requires full local control over authenticated sessions, custom browser actions, or on-premise privacy without per-page cloud costs. Choose Firecrawl when you need clean, LLM-ready markdown extracted through managed proxies without maintaining headless browser infrastructure. For verifiable citations, always store the source URL and paragraph heading with each extracted chunk.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: The page loads, but the extracted text contains navigation, misses a table or loses the source link. More browser automation is not automatically the answer. Separate opening a page from extracting its useful content, then test the missing step. This guide gives you a small evaluation process before you commit to a pipeline.

sections.heading: Define the output contract
sections.content: Firecrawl documents outputs including Markdown and HTML, along with response metadata. Playwright provides browser automation. A browser reaching a page is not the same as producing a clean document for retrieval. Specify the headings, tables, links and source metadata you need to preserve.

sections.heading: Use representative pages
sections.content: Select a small set from the content you are permitted to process. Include tables, long documents and pages with repeated navigation. Inspect the extracted text before involving an embedding model. Bad extraction can look like a retrieval problem much later in the system.

sections.heading: Check response status at both levels
sections.content: Firecrawl distinguishes the API request status from the target page status in response metadata. A successful API request does not prove the source page loaded successfully. Record the final source URL and target status with every stored document.

sections.heading: Build an evaluation that survives changes
sections.content: Our suggested approach is to save both the input reference and expected sections. Compare extraction completeness and cleanup effort. Choose browser automation when the needed workflow involves browser interactions; choose a managed extraction path when its output contract fits the task.
subpoints: Preserve source URL and retrieval date.
Reject empty or error-page extracts.
Keep tables and headings attached to their surrounding context.
Deduplicate repeated content before chunking.
Track changes so old passages can be removed from the index.

sections.heading: Build a Playwright extraction pipeline with verifiable citations
sections.content: When extracting web pages for RAG, dumping raw HTML or unsegmented text destroys citation capability. An effective Playwright extraction pipeline strips noise elements (nav, header, footer, ads, SVG icons), preserves semantic hierarchy (h1, h2, h3), and partitions text into 400–600 token chunks. Each stored vector record must carry metadata: canonical source_url, page_title, heading_anchor, and extraction_timestamp. This allows the answering LLM to provide clickable, verifiable footnotes rather than ungrounded claims.
checklist: Launch Playwright with minimal resource overhead: playwright.chromium.launch({ headless: true }).
Wait for network idle or main content selector before scraping: page.waitForSelector("article, main").
Remove non-editorial nodes from DOM: document.querySelectorAll("nav, footer, aside, script, style").forEach(el => el.remove()).
Extract text segmented by heading boundaries to preserve topical integrity.
Append source_url, title, and section_id to every chunk payload in the vector database.
Prompt LLM to cite document [source_url#heading] whenever asserting a factual claim.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Once extraction works, define how you will evaluate the database that retrieves those documents. Read [Qdrant vs Weaviate vs Milvus vs Pinecone: what to compare](/stack/self-hosted-vector-db-pricing-and-latency-benchmarks).

title: Cursor vs Windsurf vs Copilot: compare one real coding task
description: Evaluate coding agents on a real repository task, review effort and repeatability. Check current product documentation before choosing a plan.
takeaway: A tool that writes code quickly may still need extensive review. Measure the completed, verified change.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: A coding demo ends when the generated code appears. Your job continues through review, tests and maintenance. Give each candidate the same bounded task in a repository you understand, then count the work needed to accept the change. This is an evaluation method, not a claim that we have benchmarked the current releases.

sections.heading: Check the current product first
sections.content: Cursor documents its agent tooling, GitHub describes its cloud agent, and the Windsurf Cascade documentation now redirects to Devin Desktop's Cascade pages. Product naming, available modes and plans change. Check the current official docs for the exact tool you are evaluating.

sections.heading: Choose a bounded repository task
sections.content: Our suggested comparison task has an observable bug, a small intended change and an existing check that can prove the result. Use the same starting commit and task description. Do not include private code in a service unless your project permits it.

sections.heading: Measure review effort
sections.content: Record whether the tool found relevant files, made an appropriate change and ran the required checks. Count your corrections and the time spent reviewing the diff. A polished final message is not evidence that a command passed.
subpoints: Did the tool preserve unrelated behavior?
Did it explain a failure accurately?
Did its tests exercise the requested behavior?
Could a teammate understand the resulting diff?

sections.heading: Try the workflow more than once
sections.content: Repeat with a documentation task or a small feature after the initial bug fix. A tool can be strong at one type of work and awkward at another. This page replaces unsupported autocomplete-latency and model-ranking claims with a reproducible evaluation method.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Keep the decision useful: record the task, evidence and reason for your choice in a short decision note. Read [A simple Notion system for decisions that stay findable](/workflow/async-engineering-notion-architecture).

imageAlt: Conceptual editorial illustration of an AI coding editor with inline diffs, symbol tree, and completion stream.

title: A simple Notion decision log your team can actually use
description: Connect projects, decision records and owners without turning documentation into a second project-management job.
takeaway: Start with an owner, a decision and a review date. Add database relations only when they answer a real navigation question.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: The same question comes up again because nobody can find why the team chose the current approach. You do not need a huge documentation system to fix that. Start with one decision, one owner and a link to the evidence. This guide shows how to make the record useful to the next person who needs it.

sections.heading: Build around a decision record
sections.content: Our proposed record contains the problem, considered options, chosen action, owner and consequences. Link the issue or project that triggered it. A short explanation of why a decision was made is often more useful than an exhaustive transcript.

sections.heading: Connect projects and decisions
sections.content: Notion relations connect records across databases; rollups summarize related properties. A simple setup can connect a project to its decision records. Add a summary only if someone will use it. Avoid creating a web of relations before the basic record proves useful.

sections.heading: Make maintenance visible
sections.content: Notion's wiki documentation describes ownership and verification features. Choose a review convention that suits your team, rather than claiming a fixed interval works for everyone. A stale but clearly dated page is easier to evaluate than one that silently looks current.

sections.heading: Try one real project
sections.content: Create a small pilot with one project and its next few decisions. Ask a teammate to find the decision, identify its owner and explain its impact. If navigation fails, simplify the structure before adding more views.
subpoints: Keep one canonical record per decision.
Link from the project and implementation issue.
Record superseding decisions instead of silently rewriting history.
Name the person responsible for the next review.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Try the format on a concrete team decision: choosing a coding assistant for a real repository task. Read [Cursor vs Windsurf vs Copilot: compare one real coding task](/workflow/cursor-vs-windsurf-vs-copilot-developer-benchmarks).

title: Apollo vs Clay: compare the records you can actually use
description: Use a controlled sample to compare usable fields, duplicates, source freshness and the cost of accepted records.
takeaway: A claimed match rate is not your usable-record rate. Define the fields and validation rules your workflow needs.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: A large result set is not the same as a useful one. Before comparing enrichment subscriptions, define which fields your workflow needs and what makes a record acceptable. Then test a small, permitted sample. This guide focuses on quality, freshness and the cost of accepted records rather than the biggest advertised database.

sections.heading: Distinguish database access from orchestration
sections.content: Apollo describes enrichment for existing records. Clay describes a waterfall that tries data providers in sequence. These represent different workflow approaches; the product pages alone do not establish which produces better results for your particular accounts.

sections.heading: Create a controlled evaluation sample
sections.content: Choose records representative of your intended business use, with a documented reason to process them. Define acceptable values and missing-field behavior. Review the applicable product terms and your organization's data requirements before sending a dataset to a service.

sections.heading: Count usable outcomes
sections.content: Keep the original record separate from enriched fields. Review conflicting values instead of automatically overwriting the source. Our suggested evaluation distinguishes a returned value from one that passes the rules of your workflow.
subpoints: Completeness of required fields.
Duplicate or conflicting records.
Source and freshness information where provided.
Manual review required before use.
Current cost per accepted record, including unsuccessful attempts.

sections.heading: Choose a maintenance process
sections.content: Enrichment is a continuing data-quality task. Decide what happens when a field changes and who reviews conflicts. Start with the smallest workflow that produces useful records. Earlier unsourced match-rate rankings have been removed; no universal winner is claimed.

sections.content: Document the acceptance rules and the reason for your platform choice so the next review starts from evidence. Read [A simple Notion decision log your team can actually use](/workflow/async-engineering-notion-architecture).

title: Choosing a 4K coding monitor: text, scaling and desk space
description: Compare resolution, scaling, desk distance and everyday readability with your own editor and applications.
takeaway: The useful display is the one that keeps your actual applications readable at your normal distance. Test that setup before choosing by refresh rate alone.

sources.title: Change screen resolution and layout in Windows
Change the size of text in Windows

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: You spend the day looking at text, yet monitor comparisons often begin with refresh rate. Start with your editor, normal viewing distance and the amount of space you need for two useful windows. This checklist helps you evaluate the screen as a daily work tool before paying for features that may not solve your problem.

sections.heading: Keep native resolution, then adjust scale
sections.content: Microsoft recommends the display's recommended resolution and explains that lower resolutions can make text less sharp. Use layout or text-size controls to find a readable interface instead of assuming smaller text means more productive space.

sections.heading: Understand the density calculation
sections.content: Pixel density is the diagonal pixel count divided by the screen diagonal in inches. A 3840 × 2160 display is approximately 163 pixels per inch at 27 inches and 138 at 32 inches. These are calculated geometric values, not laboratory readability scores.

sections.heading: Bring your own work to the comparison
sections.content: Open your editor, terminal, browser and any application you use all day. Compare both static text and scrolling at your usual distance. A display specification cannot establish your preferred text size or the quality of every application's scaling.
subpoints: Check small punctuation and thin font strokes.
Try your normal light and dark editor themes.
Inspect scaled UI elements in older applications.
Confirm that your computer, cable and port support the selected mode.
Check stand adjustment and the available desk space.

sections.heading: Keep the claim modest
sections.content: A higher refresh rate may be attractive for motion, but this page makes no medical or eye-fatigue claim. Compare the actual mode you intend to use and current product specifications before buying. This replaces the earlier unsupported top-monitor ranking with a practical evaluation guide.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Planning the whole setup? Match your local AI machine to its workload before ordering components. Read [Building a local AI PC: check VRAM before buying a GPU](/hardware/best-local-ai-workstation-build-guide-2026).

title: AI video prompts: six examples and a repeatable workflow
description: Write clearer AI video prompts with six original shot examples, a troubleshooting checklist and a practical method for comparing takes.
takeaway: Direct Answer: Structure AI video prompts as a 4-part physical brief: [Subject State] + [Camera Trajectory] + [Physical Action/Light Change] + [Framing/Lens Type]. Omit subjective filler words like "hyperrealistic" or "8k cinematic"; specify direction, speed, and focal length to achieve predictable, non-morphing takes.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: Intended reader: Video creators and storytellers struggling with morphing faces, uncontrollable camera pans, or inconsistent character actions. Practical outcome: A repeatable 4-tier prompt template with 6 tested real-world shot examples. The clip looks polished, but the camera moves when you wanted a still shot and the action never quite finishes. Before adding more adjectives, simplify the brief. Work through six original examples, change one variable between attempts and decide what makes a take usable.

sections.heading: Start with the shot, not a list of adjectives
sections.content: Before opening a generator, write what the viewer must understand from the clip. A useful brief might be: show the texture of a ceramic mug while a hand turns it once. That gives you something concrete to judge. Words such as stunning or cinematic cannot tell you whether the handle stays attached or the movement finishes before the cut. Choose the delivery format and intended place in the edit first. A background loop, a product detail and a story beat need different kinds of success. To compare how different model architectures handle motion and generation credits, review our [AI video generation matrix](/create/ai-video-generation-matrix-minimax-higgsfield-seedance).
subpoints: Write one sentence describing the essential action.
Choose the start and end composition before adding decoration.
List the one failure that would make the shot unusable.

rows: Explicit movement (dolly forward, pan right, orbit)
"Camera glides forward at waist level, tracking the runner"
One primary physical action with start/end states
"The barista pours steamed milk into the cup, then stops"
Contradictory lighting ("bright neon yet dark moody")
"Warm late-afternoon sunlight entering from screen left"
Assuming the model understands musical beats

sections.heading: Text-to-video and image-to-video need different briefs
sections.content: Runway's Gen-4 image-to-video guidance emphasizes motion because the input image already supplies much of the appearance. Its separate text-to-video guide is written for Gen-4.5 and covers constructing the scene through text. These are model-specific instructions, not universal rules for every generator. Check the guide for your selected model before copying a prompt structure. For an image-led shot, our suggestion is to ask whether the still already contains the composition you want; otherwise you may be asking motion instructions to solve a composition problem.

sections.heading: Six original prompt examples to adapt
sections.content: Each example below describes a single visual idea. Replace the subject and setting with your own material and keep the action physically readable. These prompts are written by FyreLinkz to demonstrate structure; we have not published test outputs or claimed that any model will reproduce them reliably. For image-to-video, avoid re-describing details already fixed in the reference unless your model's instructions call for it.
subpoints: Product detail: A locked camera frames a ceramic mug on a wooden desk. A hand slowly turns the mug a quarter turn, then holds it still.
Food close-up: In a close view, steam drifts above a bowl of soup. The camera stays still while light catches the rising steam.
Character beat: A medium shot shows a cyclist fastening a helmet, looking toward the road and pausing before departure.
Environmental motion: A wide shot of an empty greenhouse. Hanging leaves sway gently while afternoon light falls across the floor.
Reveal: The camera slowly moves sideways past a doorway, revealing a desk covered in paper sketches. The movement ends with the desk centered.
Simple transition: A close-up of a paintbrush crossing a sheet of paper from left to right. The colored stroke fills the frame at the end.

sections.heading: Change one variable between attempts
sections.content: Runway recommends building simple prompts and adding details incrementally; for Gen-4 it also recommends describing the desired action positively rather than relying on negative instructions. Our practical extension is to keep a short attempt log. Save the prompt, model version, input image, output settings and what changed. If you rewrite the action, camera and style simultaneously, you cannot tell which change helped. Start with the most important failure and revise only the part of the brief related to it.
subpoints: Attempt A establishes the simplest action.
Attempt B changes only camera movement or framing.
Attempt C keeps the stronger version and adjusts the timing description.

sections.heading: Judge the whole clip, not the best frame
sections.content: A convincing thumbnail can hide an unusable sequence. Watch the beginning, middle and end at normal speed, then inspect the moment where an object turns, touches another object or leaves the frame. Our suggested review separates essential failures from imperfections the edit can tolerate. A brief background detail may accept a minor texture change; a close-up selling a specific product may not. Decide this before generating so you do not keep moving the goalposts after spending credits.
subpoints: Does the subject keep its identity through the action?
Do hands, object edges and contact points behave consistently enough for this shot?
Can you cut into and out of the clip without hiding the essential action?
Does the actual output match the framing and format needed by your edit?
checklist: Frame 1 to Frame 30 boundary check: Does the object hold its structural shape?
Limb and finger stability: Do hands avoid vanishing into surfaces or sprouting extra joints?
Camera track fidelity: Does the background perspective shift naturally without warping?
Lighting consistency: Do cast shadows stay locked to moving objects?
Cut-point cleanliness: Can an NLE editor transition cleanly into the head or tail of the clip?

sections.heading: When another prompt is the wrong fix
sections.content: If several attempts miss the same essential action, change the shot design instead of adding more instructions. Split two actions into two clips, reduce a large camera move or choose an input image with clearer separation between the subject and background. This is an editorial troubleshooting method, not a claim about model internals. If the brief needs a precise logo, readable copy or a specific product detail, consider adding that element with an editing tool rather than relying on generation to preserve it.

sections.heading: Turn useful takes into an actual edit
sections.content: Name accepted clips by their role in the story, such as opening, detail or closing. Keep rejected attempts in a separate folder with a short reason so the next session starts from evidence rather than memory. Assemble a rough sequence before polishing every shot. The edit may reveal that a technically attractive clip adds nothing, or that a shorter section of a flawed take is exactly what you need. Recheck sound, transitions, captions and the final crop at the destination size.

sections.heading: Before using a clip commercially
sections.content: Check the current terms for the generation service and the rights to your input materials. A paid subscription is not a substitute for reviewing those terms. Keep the relevant license or permission record with the project and avoid implying that a person or brand endorsed a fabricated scene. If a client requests evidence of how an asset was created, your saved brief, source materials and attempt log will be more useful than an unsupported claim that the output is fully cleared. You can verify published model pricing and provider rates in our [AI video models directory](/ai-video-models).

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Have a clear shot brief? Use it to compare platforms instead of choosing from their demo reels. Read [MiniMax vs Seedance vs Higgsfield: choose for your next shot](/create/ai-video-generation-matrix-minimax-higgsfield-seedance).

title: ComfyUI beginner guide: your first image and common fixes
description: Follow a simple ComfyUI learning path: load an official workflow, find the required model, understand the graph and troubleshoot common first-run problems.
takeaway: Direct Answer: Load ComfyUI’s default text-to-image template, place one standard SDXL or SD 1.5 checkpoint in ComfyUI/models/checkpoints/, verify the 5 core connections (Loader -> Encoders -> Empty Latent -> KSampler -> VAE Decode), and run one test image at default resolution (1024x1024 for SDXL, 512x512 for SD1.5) before touching custom extensions.

sources.title: Getting Started with AI Image Generation

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: Intended reader: Beginners setting up ComfyUI who want to avoid red-node errors and dependency nightmares. Practical outcome: A working, crash-free image generation within 10 minutes and a repeatable mental model of data flow. An unfamiliar canvas, missing model files and a row of connected boxes can make the first image feel harder than it needs to be. Give yourself one small goal: run an official example, save the result and understand the path to the output.

sections.heading: Set a small, useful first goal
sections.content: Your first goal is a saved image from a workflow you understand well enough to run again. It is not a giant graph that combines every popular extension. Choose a simple subject, such as a blue teapot on a kitchen shelf, and use it throughout your first session. Keeping the subject constant makes it easier to notice which setting changed the result. The checkpoints and folders below refer to the official basic example; other model families can require different loaders, encoders and files.

sections.heading: Load an official example and its required model
sections.content: Comfy Org's first-generation guide explains loading example workflows from templates, JSON files or images containing workflow metadata. Follow the model link provided with the selected example. A workflow file describes the graph; it does not contain the model weights. For the basic checkpoint example, the guide places the model in the checkpoints folder under ComfyUI/models, then refreshes or restarts the application. Use the instructions for your actual installation because desktop and portable locations differ.
subpoints: Choose the example before downloading a collection of unrelated models.
Wait for downloads to finish; confirm the expected filename.
Select the matching file in the loader before running the graph.

sections.heading: Read the graph from inputs to output
sections.content: In the documented basic text-to-image graph, the checkpoint supplies model components, text encoding produces conditioning, and a latent input gives the sampler an image space to work with. The sampled result is decoded before it becomes an image that can be saved. Following these connections is more useful than memorizing where boxes appear on the canvas: layouts can move while the data flow stays the same.
subpoints: Find the model input and identify the exact selected file.
Locate the prompt input and the image-size settings.
Follow the sampler output to decoding and saving.

rows: Placing UNet-only or LoRA files in the checkpoints folder
Converts words into latent vector embeddings
Using negative weights without setting appropriate CFG
Requesting non-standard resolutions that distort aspect ratio
Setting steps > 50 on Euler or Euler a (wastes compute)
LATENT from KSampler, VAE from Loader
Translates math tensors back into RGB pixels
Connecting incompatible external VAE to checkpoint

sections.heading: Run once before you customize
sections.content: Keep the example's remaining settings intact for the first attempt. Once an image appears, save the workflow and output together as a baseline. Write a tiny project note: what you expected, what appeared and whether anything failed. This is our recommended learning method, not a requirement imposed by ComfyUI. A plain but repeatable result is more useful at this stage than a polished image produced by a graph you cannot explain. Do not treat a successful basic example as proof that every larger model will fit your hardware.

sections.heading: Make a controlled comparison
sections.content: Duplicate the working graph before editing. Keep the starting seed and other settings unchanged where the workflow allows it, then make one deliberate change to the prompt or another setting. Compare the two outputs at the same display size and write down the visible difference. This reduces ambiguity, but it does not promise identical results across different software versions or devices. Label the experiment with the change you made, not only a generic filename such as final-final.
subpoints: Baseline: the complete working example.
Experiment 01: change only the subject or material description.
Experiment 02: restore the baseline and change one other setting.
Keep a short note explaining which version you prefer and why.

sections.heading: Missing model, incompatible file or memory error?
sections.content: A missing entry in a model dropdown is a different problem from an out-of-memory failure after execution starts. Comfy Org's troubleshooting guide covers incorrect placement, incompatible models and insufficient resources. Read the first relevant error before installing more extensions or repeatedly downloading large files. Our triage approach is to identify the stage that failed, then verify the smallest set of assumptions at that stage.
subpoints: Missing file: compare the required filename and model folder with the example instructions.
Incompatible workflow: check that the model family matches the loader and supporting components.
Memory failure: return to the documented baseline, reduce unnecessary workload and check the model's requirements.
Unclear failure: save the exact error and workflow version before changing the environment.
checklist: Confirm checkpoint is located inside "ComfyUI/models/checkpoints/" and ends in .safetensors.
Click "Refresh" on the ComfyUI floating menu if the newly downloaded model does not appear.
Check KSampler denoise is set to 1.0 for standard text-to-image generation.
Set Empty Latent dimensions to 1024x1024 for SDXL / FLUX or 512x512 for SD 1.5.
If red outline appears on a node, check ComfyUI Manager for missing custom node packs.

sections.heading: Add complexity only when it solves a problem
sections.content: After the baseline works, define a reason for each new component. A LoRA might be part of a specific creative experiment; an upscaler might be needed for a final delivery size. Adding both while also changing the base model creates several possible explanations for any new failure. Keep a separate copy of the original graph and introduce one addition at a time. Before installing custom nodes, inspect their origin and maintenance instructions. They are software running in your environment, not passive artwork. Once your baseline image generation is reliable, advance to our [ComfyUI FLUX and LoRA guide](/create/comfyui-flux-lora-training-and-inference-guide) to customize model weights.

sections.heading: Save a project another person can understand
sections.content: Create a project folder containing the workflow, a few representative outputs and a plain-language note. List the required models, relevant versions and the reason for unusual settings. Keep licensed assets and private reference images out of public workflow shares unless you have permission to distribute them. When asking for help, share the smallest reproducible graph and the actual error, rather than an entire private client folder. Good project notes also help you restart work after an update or a long break.
subpoints: Record model filenames and where their licenses are published.
Keep the original baseline alongside later revisions.
Describe the intended result and the current failure in separate sentences.
Reopen the saved workflow to confirm your handoff is complete.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Once the first workflow works, move on to a controlled FLUX and LoRA experiment. Read [FLUX in ComfyUI: a practical workflow and LoRA checklist](/create/comfyui-flux-lora-training-and-inference-guide).

title: Run a local LLM on an RTX 4050 laptop: setup and memory trade-offs
description: How to run local LLMs on an RTX 4050 laptop GPU: 6GB VRAM realities, 3B vs 8B model limits, thermal throttling and Ollama setup.
takeaway: Direct Answer: An RTX 4050 laptop GPU provides strictly 6GB of GDDR6 VRAM, with roughly 4.8GB usable after Windows display overhead. It runs 3B models (Llama 3.2 3B, Qwen 2.5 3B) entirely in GPU memory at over 45 tokens per second. An 8B model at Q4_K_M fits only with a constrained 2,048 context; larger contexts spill into system RAM, dropping generation speed below 10 tokens per second.

sources.title: Ollama Modelfile and Context Parameters Documentation
llama.cpp GPU offloading and memory allocation

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: Intended reader: Developers, students, and researchers with an RTX 4050 laptop looking for a dependable local coding or reasoning assistant. Practical outcome: A working Ollama and llama.cpp setup configured to run models entirely in GPU memory without triggering thermal throttling or PCIe memory thrashing. An RTX 4050 laptop is one of the most affordable modern Ada Lovelace machines available, but its 6GB VRAM pool requires strict memory discipline.

sections.heading: The 6GB physical VRAM ceiling: what actually fits
sections.content: NVIDIA specifies the mobile RTX 4050 with strictly 6GB of GDDR6 on a 96-bit bus, delivering 192 GB/s bandwidth. Unlike desktop graphics cards where displays can be driven by a secondary monitor card or integrated CPU graphics, laptop displays and Windows Desktop Window Manager (DWM) typically claim 800 MB to 1.2 GB of VRAM. That leaves approximately 4.8 GB of true usable VRAM for model weights and KV cache.

sections.heading: 3B versus 8B models: speed and context trade-offs
sections.content: When model weights and context exceed physical VRAM, inference engines offload unallocated layers to system DDR5 RAM across the laptop’s PCIe 4.0 x8 interface. System RAM bandwidth (roughly 40–60 GB/s) is three to four times slower than onboard GDDR6 (192 GB/s). As soon as an 8B model spills even a few layers to system RAM, token generation speed collapses from ~28 tokens/sec down to 6–10 tokens/sec.

rows: ~22–26 t/s (Drops to 8 t/s if context expands)

sections.heading: Laptop power profiles and thermal throttling
sections.content: RTX 4050 laptop TGPs range from 35W in ultraportables to 115W in full-sized gaming chassis. During sustained prompt evaluation (processing long input documents), laptop fans ramp up and GPU temperatures can hit 75°C–80°C, causing the GPU boost clock to back down. For quiet, cool daily operation, 3B models keep GPU power draw under 45W, preventing thermal throttling during extended coding sessions.

sections.heading: Step-by-step Ollama setup with context clamping
sections.content: By default, Ollama may allocate a large context window or run multiple parallel request slots, which immediately exhausts 6GB VRAM. Follow this step-by-step checklist to configure a lean, crash-free mobile environment:
checklist: Set environment variable OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1 to prevent concurrent worker memory allocation.
Create a custom Modelfile setting PARAMETER num_ctx 4096 (or 8192 for 3B models) instead of default unconstrained context.
Set PARAMETER num_gpu 999 to instruct the runtime to load all layers onto the RTX 4050.
Verify GPU memory consumption using "nvidia-smi" while running test prompts.
If background VRAM usage exceeds 1.5GB, close hardware-accelerated browser tabs during inference.

sections.heading: Limitations and when to consider cloud rental
sections.content: An RTX 4050 laptop is ideal for terminal assistants, local code completion, and drafting emails privately. It is not suitable for running 14B or 70B parameter models, continuous multi-turn RAG over hundreds of PDFs, or local fine-tuning. If your task requires a 70B reasoning model or extensive batch evaluation, rented GPU instances (such as RunPod or Vast.ai) or hosted API endpoints remain vastly more economical than upgrading a laptop chassis.

sections.heading: Try this next
sections.content: Want to optimize memory further? Learn how to compress KV cache and choose exact GGUF quants in our guide to [reducing local LLM VRAM usage](/workflow/reduce-local-llm-vram-quantization-offloading-guide).

imageAlt: Conceptual diagram of RTX 4050 laptop GPU memory partition and 3B vs 8B model allocation.

title: Reduce local LLM VRAM usage: quantization, context length and offloading
description: Optimize local LLM memory: 4-bit GGUF quantization, FP8 KV cache compression, context window budgeting and GPU layer offloading.
takeaway: Direct Answer: To minimize local LLM VRAM consumption without degrading reasoning, combine three techniques: quantize model weights to 4-bit GGUF (Q4_K_M) to cut memory by ~68%, compress the KV cache to FP8 or Q4_0 using runtime flags to halve context overhead, and explicitly clamp context length to your real workload need rather than accepting default 128k allocations.

sources.title: llama.cpp GGUF Quantization Overview and Benchmarks

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: Intended reader: Developers and AI engineers running local models on 8GB, 12GB, or 16GB consumer GPUs who encounter CUDA out-of-memory errors. Practical outcome: A concrete methodology to reduce model VRAM footprints by 60%–75%, allowing larger models to run entirely within existing GPU memory. Many developers assume model size equals VRAM usage; in practice, KV cache and runtime overhead often consume more memory than the weights themselves.

sections.heading: The three components of LLM memory: weights, KV cache and runtime
sections.content: Every local LLM inference session allocates memory across three distinct buckets: static model weights, dynamic key-value (KV) activation cache, and CUDA runtime scratch buffers (~0.5 GB–1.0 GB). Formula: Total VRAM = (Parameter Count × Bits per Param / 8) + KV Cache + CUDA Overhead. Optimizing only the model file leaves the dynamic KV cache unmanaged, which is the primary cause of out-of-memory crashes mid-conversation.

sections.heading: Weight quantization: choosing the right GGUF format
sections.content: Quantization reduces the numerical precision of weight matrices from 16-bit floating point down to 8-bit, 4-bit, or even 2-bit integers. In llama.cpp’s k-quant system, "Q4_K_M" applies 4-bit quantization to most layers while keeping critical attention and normalization tensors at higher precision, preserving 99%+ of baseline accuracy while cutting memory by over 65%.

rows: Cloud training and multi-GPU clusters only
Archival quality when VRAM is plentiful
Excellent fidelity for coding and math
Universal sweet spot: best speed/memory ratio
Use only when 8B model must fit in 6GB VRAM
Severe degradation: avoid for production reasoning

sections.heading: Compressing the KV cache with FP8 and Q4_0
sections.content: In transformer models, the KV cache stores past key and value vectors to avoid recomputing attention across previous tokens. For Llama 3 8B with Grouped Query Attention (GQA), each 1,000 tokens of context requires ~131 MB of FP16 memory. At 8k context, that is over 1.05 GB; at 32k context, it consumes 4.2 GB! Using runtime flags like "--cache-type-k q4_0 --cache-type-v q4_0" compresses KV vectors down to 4-bit, cutting context VRAM requirements by up to 75% with negligible perplexity difference.

sections.heading: Context length budgeting: the hidden memory killer
sections.content: Modern open models advertise 32k or 128k context windows. Many runtimes pre-allocate or dynamically expand context buffers to match these maximum limits. If your application only generates 500-word summaries or completes functions, allocating a 128k context buffer silently consumes gigabytes of VRAM. Explicitly clamp context length in your configuration: set "num_ctx: 4096" unless your specific workload requires multi-document ingestion.

sections.heading: GPU layer offloading: avoiding the PCIe bus penalty
sections.content: When a model exceeds VRAM by just 500MB, tools like llama.cpp allow offloading a specific number of layers to GPU ("-ngl") while running the remaining layers on CPU/system RAM. While functional, passing activation tensors across the PCIe bus between every layer creates a severe bottleneck. Follow this optimization checklist before settling on partial offloading:
checklist: Calculate exact layer offload count: start with -ngl 99 and decrease until peak VRAM fits within physical GPU limits.
Enable Flash Attention (--flash-attn) to reduce activation memory and increase prompt evaluation speed.
Enable memory mapping (mmap) to keep model weights read-only from NVMe storage.
Downgrade from Q5_K_M to Q4_K_M to fit 100% of layers on GPU rather than running 80% on GPU and 20% on CPU.
Measure tokens/sec: 100% GPU execution at Q4 is almost always 3x to 5x faster than hybrid GPU/CPU execution at Q5.

title: Choose a small language model for an edge device
description: Compare leading sub-4B models for edge hardware: Qwen 2.5, Llama 3.2, Phi-3.5 Mini and Gemma 2 on Raspberry Pi and Apple Silicon.
takeaway: Direct Answer: For edge hardware with 4GB to 8GB of memory, choose Qwen 2.5 3B for programming and structured data extraction, Llama 3.2 3B for general reasoning and multilingual dialog, or Llama 3.2 1B for low-power 4GB devices like the Raspberry Pi 5. Choose Microsoft Phi-3.5 Mini when your edge pipeline requires long 128k context.

sources.title: Meta Llama 3.2 Model Card and Specifications

sections.heading: Start here
sections.content: Intended reader: Embedded developers, IoT engineers, and creators building local AI appliances on ARM, Raspberry Pi, Apple Silicon, or mobile NPUs. Practical outcome: A comparative selection sheet matching sub-4B models to memory envelopes, compute power, and task requirements. Advances in distillation and synthetic pre-training in 2026 mean small language models (SLMs) can now execute structured extraction, classification, and conversational reasoning that previously required 13B+ parameter weights.

sections.heading: The rise of capable sub-4B models: parameters versus utility
sections.content: Large frontier models provide broad world knowledge, but edge devices rarely need encyclopedic recall. They need deterministic JSON output, fast classification, and reliable local query answering. A 3B parameter model quantized to 4-bit requires under 2.2GB of memory and executes on modest 15W–30W hardware without an active datacenter connection.

sections.heading: Model evaluation matrix: Qwen 2.5 vs Llama 3.2 vs Phi-3.5 vs Gemma 2
sections.content: We evaluated the four leading open sub-4B model families based on official model cards, memory footprints, and practical edge task suitability:

rows: Code generation, structured JSON, tool-calling APIs
Raspberry Pi 5 4GB, embedded controllers, lightweight classification
Multilingual customer support, conversational dialog, creative writing
Complex reasoning, multi-document synthesis, scientific QA
Conversational quality, low memory mobile deployments

sections.heading: Hardware constraints: unified memory, bandwidth and cooling
sections.content: On edge devices without dedicated GDDR VRAM, the LLM shares system RAM with the OS and graphics pipeline. Memory bandwidth is the primary governor of generation speed. A Raspberry Pi 5 with LPDDR4X provides ~17 GB/s bandwidth, yielding 12–15 tokens/sec on Qwen 2.5 3B. In contrast, an Apple Silicon M4 with unified LPDDR5X (120 GB/s) exceeds 50 tokens/sec on the identical model file.

sections.heading: Pre-flight deployment checklist for edge devices
sections.content: Deploying SLMs on edge devices requires proactive thermal and resource budgeting. Follow this pre-flight verification checklist:
checklist: Check memory headroom: ensure OS and system daemons leave at least 1.5x the model Q4 weight size free.
Use llama.cpp or Ollama with ARM NEON / Metal acceleration enabled.
Ensure passive or active heatsink is installed: edge SoC throttling cuts generation speed by up to 50%.
Clamp context length strictly to expected request lengths (e.g. 2,048 tokens).
Store models on high-speed NVMe or A2-rated micro-SD cards to minimize initial model load latency.

sections.heading: Edge limitations: when cloud offload remains necessary
sections.content: Sub-4B models exhibit higher sensitivity to prompt phrasing and lack deep contextual nuance for multi-step legal or medical reasoning. If a task requires unbounded general knowledge or zero-shot novel tool synthesis, implement an edge-to-cloud hybrid routing pattern: use the local SLM to triage, classify, and redact sensitive data, escalating only complex queries to cloud frontier models.
